routes.description: Establish the four claimed historical facts from early Christian materials, connect them as a cumulative evidential set, and show that divine resurrection explains that set more adequately than the proposed literary, visionary, or sociological alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources warrant burial, an empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples’ resurrection belief, and if God raising Jesus provides the best comparative explanation of those facts despite objections from historical analogy and source criticism.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest Christian sources establish all four specified facts and that God raising Jesus best explains their conjunction.

centralBridges.description: Establish an identifiable burial and the subsequent discovery of an empty tomb from sufficiently early, independent, and historically credible traditions.
Establish that individuals and groups experienced appearances of Jesus after his death using authentic early testimony and historically usable narrative sources.
Explain why the earliest disciples sincerely adopted a specific resurrection belief despite the crucifixion and the surrounding Jewish expectations.
Demonstrate comparatively that divine resurrection accounts for the combined evidence better than legendary development, cultural borrowing, visions, or belief-preservation mechanisms.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the authenticity, early dating, and historical admissibility of Pauline traditions and the relevant Gospel materials.
Show that proposed pagan and hero-story parallels lack the relevant similarity or causal connection needed to explain the earliest Christian claims.

routes.description: Deny that the surviving sources warrant the four asserted facts or the resurrection inference by applying historical analogy, literary and textual criticism, and ordinary mechanisms for visionary reports, legendary narratives, and the persistence of religious belief.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if material uncertainty remains about one or more foundational facts, or if familiar literary, cultural, visionary, or sociological processes provide sufficient alternatives to prevent divine resurrection from being established as the best historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest sources do not establish the complete factual conjunction or do not make divine resurrection its best historical explanation.

centralBridges.description: Show that the burial, empty-tomb, and appearance materials are literary, redactional, or textually uncertain enough that the asserted events are not established.
Use comparable ancient vanished-body, apotheosis, dying-and-rising, and appearance narratives to support a legendary or hagiographic account of the traditions.
Provide non-resurrection pathways for exaltation, appearance reports, and continuing faith, including visions, retrojection, syncretism, and cognitive-dissonance reduction.
Show that invoking divine action does not resolve uncertain historical claims or outperform ordinary explanations under a case-by-case evidential method.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend historical ideal-type comparison as requiring meaningful structural similarity rather than exact correspondence or direct literary copying.
Limit the evidential reach of Pauline authenticity claims, later disciple traditions, scholarly consensus, and extra-biblical notices.
